title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Baltimore, MD: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Baltimore welders and inspectors: Key Bridge and bridge-code work, the port, steel fabrication and Parts A to C.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Baltimore: Six Days of Preparation for Inspectors on Bridges, Ships and Steel
html:
Baltimore's harbor has seen steel made, ships built and bridges raised for well over a century, and in 2024 it was handed one of the largest welding jobs in the country: replacing the Francis Scott Key Bridge. Bridge work, port and marine repair, and structural fabrication all need people who can judge welds against a code and sign for the result. In most specifications that person is an AWS Certified Welding Inspector. Atlantis NDT offers Baltimore candidates a six-day course (6-day, structured around the three exam parts) to prepare for the AWS CWI examination, written for welders, fitters, QC staff, NDT technicians and engineers.

The credential itself is not ours to give. AWS issues CWI certification to candidates who pass its examination, and AWS alone decides eligibility, runs the test and scores it. This course has no approval, accreditation or endorsement from AWS; Atlantis teaches the material and nothing more. Read the national AWS CWI exam prep page for the full day-by-day syllabus and the published exam details.

Steel, ships and a bridge to rebuild

Three strands run through Baltimore's welding economy. The first is heavy steel: the Sparrows Point peninsula was home to one of the country's great steel mills, and although the mill has closed and the site has become an industrial and logistics hub, the region kept a deep pool of structural fabricators, erectors and steel trades. The second is maritime: the Port of Baltimore's terminals, ship repair along the Patapsco and the U.S. Coast Guard Yard at Curtis Bay all put marine welding to work. The third is infrastructure: tunnels, bridges and interchanges owned by state agencies, with the Key Bridge replacement now at the front of the line.

Those strands overlap. A welder who learned the trade in a structural shop may spend a season on marine repair and then take a QC job on a bridge contract. Inspectors here are expected to move between structural steel, bridge members and marine structures, which is why the code-book choice for Part C deserves real thought.

The Key Bridge replacement and the bridge welding code

When a container ship struck the Francis Scott Key Bridge in March 2024 and the span collapsed, the Maryland Transportation Authority took on the job of replacing it. A project of that size runs for years and draws on steel fabricators, erectors, testing agencies and the owner's own inspection consultants. Every structural steel weld on it is governed by a bridge welding code and the owner's contract provisions, not by building-code practice.

That code is AWS D1.5, the Bridge Welding Code, developed jointly with AASHTO. It differs from the structural steel code in ways an inspector feels daily: tighter control of welding procedures, stricter rules for preheat and consumable handling, and a fracture control plan for members whose failure would bring down the structure. Inspectors working for fabricators or for the owner need to recognize which members carry those extra requirements and what that means for testing and documentation. If bridge work is where you see yourself, D1.5 is a strong Part C choice; the AWS D1.5 overview outlines the code's structure.

The rebuild is also reshaping local training. In 2025, the Community College of Baltimore County announced a welding training center on its Dundalk campus, backed by a grant from the Baltimore Community Foundation's Maryland Tough Baltimore Strong Key Bridge Fund, and the foundation described the facility as rising in the footprint of the bridge.

The port, the Coast Guard Yard and marine work

The Port of Baltimore handles container, roll-on/roll-off and bulk cargo across several public and private terminals, and every crane rail, fender system, mooring structure and conveyor needs welded repair at some point. Ship repair and barge work along the river add steel replacement and piping jobs. The U.S. Coast Guard Yard at Curtis Bay builds and overhauls Coast Guard cutters and boats, bringing government shipbuilding specifications into the local mix.

Marine work often runs under requirements set by the vessel owner, the government or a classification society, in addition to welding codes. A CWI brings a strong grounding in processes, joint preparation, distortion and visual acceptance, but it does not replace program-specific qualifications that a yard or agency may require of its inspectors. Ask the employer what its quality program expects before you plan your path, and treat the CWI as the credential you carry between jobs.

Sparrows Point and the fabricators that followed

The mill at Sparrows Point shaped generations of Baltimore steelworkers, and its legacy is a regional supply chain that still fabricates girders, columns, plate structures, tanks and process equipment. Structural shops supplying buildings, bridges and industrial projects need inspectors for incoming material checks, fit-up, in-process monitoring and final acceptance. Many also maintain fabricator certifications whose audits look closely at how inspectors are qualified and how inspection records are kept.

For shop inspectors, the most common Part C choice is AWS D1.1, the structural welding code for steel. The AWS D1.1 overview and the guide to D1.1 weld acceptance criteria help a shop inspector see how the code's tables translate into accept-or-reject decisions on the floor.

Who hires CWIs around Baltimore

Employer typeWhat the CWI does thereCode most often in play
Bridge and structural fabricatorsIn-process and final inspection, procedure and welder records, mill certificate checksAWS D1.5 or D1.1
Steel erectors and general contractorsField weld inspection, bolting and connection checks, daily reportsAWS D1.1
Testing and inspection agenciesSpecial inspection on building projects, owner's verification on public worksAWS D1.1 and D1.5
Owner's inspection consultants on bridge contractsVerifying the contractor's quality control and keeping the owner's recordAWS D1.5 plus contract provisions
Marine repair and government shipworkStructural repairs, steel replacement, pipingOwner and program specifications alongside welding codes
Utilities and pipeline contractorsPipe welding inspection and recordsAPI 1104

Hospital, university and government building programs across the city add steady structural work, and gas main replacement keeps pipeline crews busy in the suburbs. The mix means a Baltimore CWI rarely sits idle for long between projects.

A new generation of welders: CCBC and Anne Arundel Community College

Workforce investment around the harbor has picked up sharply since the bridge collapse. Beyond the 2025 welding training center announcement, CCBC broke ground in April 2026 on a larger Welding and Trades Center at its Dundalk campus on Sollers Point Road. The college says the building will include a large welding laboratory and a virtual reality lab, with construction projected to finish in spring 2027 and courses to start there that summer. Earlbeck Gases & Technologies, a welding supplier with a facility in Rosedale, is named as a continuing training partner. Anne Arundel Community College also runs a welding program serving the southern side of the metro area.

These programs produce welders, not inspectors. The CWI comes later, once a welder has built enough documented, verifiable welding-related experience to meet AWS requirements. The number of years depends on education: five years for a candidate with a high school diploma, fewer with a welding or engineering degree, more with less schooling. The full education-and-experience table sits on the national course page. If you came through a college program, keep your certificates and transcripts: AWS gives credit for some formal education.

AWS in Maryland: District 3 and local sections

AWS organizes its local sections into districts, and Maryland falls in District 3 alongside the capital region. The Washington D.C. Section and the Cumberland Valley Section have held joint events for decades, and the Washington D.C. Section lists a certification chair among its officers, a useful contact for anyone with questions about the CWI process. Check the AWS section directory on aws.org for the section closest to Baltimore and its meeting calendar. Section meetings are where you meet inspectors who have recently taken the practical, hear which local employers are hiring, and learn about AWS Foundation scholarships.

From Baltimore to the exam room

Parts A and C are computer-based. Once AWS confirms your application, its letter carries the eligibility code you use to schedule Fundamentals and Code Application at a Prometric center, and Prometric has locations across Maryland. Part B is the hands-on practical, and AWS offers it only at its own seminar and examination venues on fixed dates, using specimens and instruments it supplies. Look up the closest Part B venue and date on aws.org first; every other date in a Baltimore study plan hangs off it.

The passing standard is 72% on each part, and AWS returns a combined report once all three are done. Before the examination you also need a current AWS vision test covering near acuity and color perception. AWS sets its own examination charges and lists them on aws.org; the CWI budget planner helps you add up the rest. To see which parts trip candidates most, read CWI results by exam part.

Six days, two ways to take them

Day one lays the vocabulary: welding processes, AWS terms, joint geometry and the welding symbol. Day two covers metallurgy, destructive tests, discontinuities and their causes, inspection methods, safety and the inspector's ethical duties. Day three rehearses the practical with gauges, weld profile measurement and visual acceptance against a set of specifications. Day four lives inside the chosen code book. Day five is timed mock exams for Fundamentals, Practical and Code, and day six goes back over weak areas and walks through exam logistics and the application paperwork.

On your own, online

A Baltimore candidate working shifts can follow the six days as a self-paced plan, with written materials, practice questions Atlantis wrote to the published topic list, timed papers, and an instructor reachable for questions. Nothing is scheduled; you decide when each day's material gets done. None of the practice questions comes from a real AWS examination.

As a company group, on site

A fabricator, erector, marine contractor or testing agency can host the six days at its own site for several employees at once. Practical work then uses the company's gauges and real welds from its own projects, and code practice can center on D1.5 for a bridge shop or D1.1 for a structural one. Each employee still submits an individual application to AWS and must personally meet the experience and vision rules.

Choosing your Part C code in Baltimore

For most Baltimore candidates the decision comes down to two books. If you work in a structural shop, for an erector, or on special inspection of buildings, choose D1.1. If your work is bridge fabrication or inspection for a transportation owner, consider D1.5, especially with the Key Bridge replacement and other state structures in the pipeline. Pipeline and utility inspectors should look at API 1104, and anyone in power or process piping should look at the ASME selection. Whichever you choose, study the edition AWS names for the examination, which can trail the newest one on the shelf, and practice finding tables quickly, because the open-book part is a race against the clock more than a memory test.

Adding NDT to a Baltimore CWI

Bridge members, crane girders and marine structures often need more than visual inspection: ultrasonic testing of groove welds, magnetic particle testing for surface cracks, and occasionally penetrant testing. Those methods are performed by technicians certified by their employer under ASNT SNT-TC-1A after training, documented experience and examination. A Baltimore CWI who adds UT or MT becomes far more useful on bridge and fabrication work. Atlantis provides SNT-TC-1A-based courses toward that; see NDT training in Baltimore, ultrasonic testing in Baltimore, ultrasonic weld inspection and magnetic particle inspection of structural steel. The VT Level 2 course and the Practical NDT welding workshop sharpen visual technique, and the free NDT practice tests help with method exams.

Keep the CWI alive once you have it. AWS frames it as a nine-year credential with renewal paperwork in the third and sixth years and recertification at nine. For a broader view of career value, read CWI requirements and career impact.

What to include in your Baltimore request

Tell us how many people the course is for, give a rough outline of each candidate's schooling and welding history, name the Part C code each expects to use, and say whether anyone has already applied to AWS or secured a practical date. For an on-site group, add the site address, the gauges and weld samples on hand, and the weeks that suit your production or project schedule. Submit it through the Baltimore CWI preparation request and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Is the course held at a Baltimore training center?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no Baltimore location; its offices are in Houston and Hyderabad. People preparing alone work online with an instructor on call, while an employer can bring the full six days to its own shop. See the course outline.
AWS. It sets the eligibility rules, runs and scores the three-part examination, and issues the certification. Atlantis prepares candidates and plays no part in the examination.

faq.q: Which code book suits inspectors on the Key Bridge replacement?
faq.a: Bridge steel is governed by AWS D1.5 plus the owner's contract provisions, so D1.5 is the natural Part C choice for bridge fabrication and owner's inspection work. See the D1.5 overview.

faq.q: I just finished a welding program at CCBC. Can I take the CWI exam?
faq.a: Not straight away. AWS requires years of documented welding-related experience, and the number depends on your education. A college program can reduce the experience needed but does not replace it; the table is on the national page.

faq.q: Where do Baltimore candidates sit the practical?
faq.a: AWS offers Part B only at its own seminar and examination venues on fixed dates. Check aws.org for the nearest one. Parts A and C are taken on computer at Prometric centers in Maryland and nearby.

faq.q: Does a CWI let me inspect on Coast Guard or Navy ships?
faq.a: Government shipwork runs under its own specifications, and yards qualify inspectors under their own programs. The CWI is a strong personal credential, but check what the specific yard requires.
AWS lists 72% as the minimum on each of the three parts. Results come back as one combined report.

faq.q: Are the practice questions real AWS questions?
faq.a: No. Every question is original, written by Atlantis to the published body of knowledge. Atlantis never sees AWS examination content.

faq.q: Is there an AWS section for Baltimore?
faq.a: Maryland is in AWS District 3. The Washington D.C. and Cumberland Valley sections are active in the region; check the AWS section directory on aws.org for the section nearest you.
We quote each request individually. AWS lists its own examination charges on aws.org, and the budget planner covers the other items. Ask for a quote.
